title: Recent advances in pharmacological research on Ecklonia species: a review

subsections.content:
The clinical relevance of Ecklonia-derived pharmacology is underscored by the expanding global burden of chronic, multifactorial disorders in which oxidative stress, metabolic dysregulation, inflammation, and tissue injury are central pathogenic drivers. Diabetes has long been recognized as a rapidly growing epidemic, with global prevalence projected to increase from 2.8% in 2000 to 4.4% by 2030 and the number of affected individuals from 171 to 366 million, even under conservative assumptions ref [4]. Obesity, a major upstream risk factor for insulin resistance, cardiovascular disease, and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, has similarly emerged as a worldwide epidemic shaped by urbanization, caloric excess, and reduced physical activity ref [7].

A parallel demographic transition is occurring in age-related neurological disease. Population aging is expected to markedly increase mortality from neurodegenerative disorders; early projections for the United States estimated substantial rises in deaths from dementia, Parkinson’s disease, and motor neuron disease over coming decades ref [5]. Contemporary epidemiology has further confirmed the accelerating prevalence and societal cost of dementia worldwide, while chronic neuroinflammation and oxidative injury remain key therapeutic targets ref [8], ref [9]. These trends are particularly relevant for marine phlorotannins because many reported Ecklonia activities converge on antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anti-apoptotic, and cytoprotective mechanisms.

Beyond diabetes and neurodegeneration, obesity-associated liver injury, allergic inflammation, and chronic tissue damage collectively drive major morbidity and healthcare expenditure. The convergence of these conditions on shared molecular pathways—including ROS overproduction, NF-kappaB activation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and cytokine imbalance—creates a strong rationale for surveying Ecklonia species as a multi-target marine bioresource. Accordingly, this review focuses on recent pharmacological studies that position Ecklonia metabolites, especially phlorotannins, as candidates for adjunctive prevention or therapy across metabolic, hepatic, neuroinflammatory, allergic, and tissue-protective indications ref [4], ref [5], ref [7].

subsections.subsection_title: Marine Brown Algae and Phlorotannins as a Bioactive Resource
subsections.content:
Marine brown algae constitute a chemically distinctive pharmacological reservoir because they accumulate both polyphenolic metabolites and structurally diverse sulfated polysaccharides, notably fucoidans, in addition to pigments and sterols. Broad reviews of marine algal glycans have emphasized that these macromolecules show substantial bioactivity and translational potential in nutraceutical, cosmetic, and pharmaceutical settings ref [4]. Within Ecklonia species, this resource is especially notable because phlorotannins occur at comparatively high levels and coexist with fucose-rich polysaccharides, creating a multi-component matrix with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anticoagulant, and metabolic activities.

The principal low-molecular-weight signatures of Ecklonia are phlorotannins, a class of brown-algal polyphenols biosynthesized through phloroglucinol polymerization. Eckol, dieckol, bieckols, phlorofucofuroeckol-A, and 6,6′-bieckol have been repeatedly isolated from Ecklonia cava, E. stolonifera, and E. kurome, and are now regarded as core chemotaxonomic and pharmacological markers of the genus ref [2], ref [3], ref [4], ref [5], ref [6], ref [7]. These compounds exhibit marked structural diversity in aryl–aryl and dibenzodioxin linkages, a feature that likely underlies their broad target engagement across redox, inflammatory, enzymatic, and signaling pathways ref [3], ref [6], ref [8].

Equally important, brown algal cell walls provide fucoidans and related fucose-containing sulfated polysaccharides whose composition varies with species, harvest conditions, and extraction protocol ref [4], ref [9], ref [10]. In Ecklonia kurome, anticoagulant fucans were among the earliest functionally characterized constituents, and their activity was shown to depend on sulfate content and molecular size ref [11], ref [12], ref [13]. Thus, Ecklonia should be viewed not as a source of a single lead compound, but as a modular marine bioresource in which phlorotannins and sulfated polysaccharides together shape the genus’ unusually broad pharmacological profile and justify its central place in recent marine drug research ref [4], ref [9], ref [14].

Oxidative injury is a central mechanism linking many of the reported bioactivities of Ecklonia species, particularly their phlorotannin-rich extracts and purified constituents. In cellular systems, an ethanol extract of Ecklonia cava showed clear cytoprotection against oxidative stress, associated with activation of MAPK signaling and induction of the Nrf2-dependent antioxidant enzymes heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) and NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase-1 (NQO-1) ref [6]. This is consistent with broader observations that Ecklonia-derived phlorotannins act as ROS-scavenging polyphenols and strengthen endogenous antioxidant defenses rather than functioning solely as direct radical quenchers.

At the level of defined compounds, several studies highlight structure-dependent protection from oxidative insults. Fucodiphlorethol G purified from E. cava suppressed ultraviolet B-induced oxidative stress and cellular damage, supporting a role for Ecklonia phlorotannins in photoprotection and membrane/DNA preservation under ROS-generating conditions ref [7]. Closely related evidence with phloroglucinol and eckol indicates protection of cultured cells from oxidative injury and supports the view that low-molecular-weight phlorotannin building blocks can mediate meaningful cytoprotection in addition to larger oligomers ref [5] ref [6].

These antioxidant properties extend to radioprotection in vivo. Eckol improved survival in lethally irradiated mice, reduced lymphocyte DNA damage, and promoted hematopoietic and immune recovery after whole-body irradiation, indicating multi-level protection beyond simple radical scavenging ref [9]. In the gastrointestinal tract, both phloroglucinol and eckol increased jejunal crypt survival and reduced radiation-induced apoptosis in mice ref [5]. A later mechanistic study further showed that phloroglucinol preserved intestinal architecture while downregulating p53, Bax, and Bak and restoring Bcl-2/Bcl-XS/L expression, thereby raising the apoptotic threshold in irradiated crypt cells ref [6]. Together, these studies position Ecklonia phlorotannins as promising leads for mitigating oxidative tissue injury, especially in contexts of radiation exposure and epithelial barrier damage ref [5] ref [9] ref [6].

Ecklonia species have attracted particular interest in metabolic disease because their extracts and phlorotannins target multiple nodes of glucose and lipid homeostasis. In vivo, gametophytes of Ecklonia kurome lowered circulating glucose and triacylglycerol in diabetic and prediabetic mouse models, supporting a broader antihyperglycemic and hypotriglyceridemic potential beyond mature thallus extracts ref [12]. At the compound level, phlorotannins from E. stolonifera and E. bicyclis inhibit both protein tyrosine phosphatase 1B and α-glucosidase, providing a mechanistic basis for improving insulin signaling and delaying carbohydrate digestion ref [17]. Consistently, a phlorotannin constituent of E. cava, 2,7″-phloroglucinol-6,6′-bieckol, markedly suppressed α-glucosidase/α-amylase activity and reduced postprandial glucose excursions in streptozotocin-induced diabetic mice ref [16].

The hepatoprotective literature is similarly compelling. E. stolonifera extract attenuated ethanol-induced fatty liver in rats ref [13], while E. cava polyphenols protected hepatocytes against ethanol injury by suppressing CYP2E1 activity, enhancing ADH and ALDH activities, and elevating cAMP in a protein kinase A-dependent manner ref [14]. In diet-induced obesity, E. cava polyphenol extract reduced body-weight gain, adipose mass, dyslipidemia, hepatic steatosis, insulin resistance, and inflammatory and oxidative stress markers, effects linked to activation of AMPK and SIRT1, decreased SREBP1c/FAS-driven lipogenesis, and enhanced β-oxidation pathways ref [15]. These findings position Ecklonia preparations as candidates for both alcoholic and metabolic fatty liver settings ref [13], ref [14], ref [15].

Anti-obesity actions also extend to adipocyte differentiation models. Fucosterol isolated from E. stolonifera inhibited adipogenesis in 3T3-L1 cells through modulation of FoxO1 signaling, with suppression of PI3K/Akt and ERK cascades and downregulation of PPARγ, C/EBPα, and SREBP-1 ref [9]. Complementarily, enzyme-treated E. cava extract suppressed lipid accumulation and reduced C/EBPα, SREBP-1c, A-FABP, FAS, and adiponectin expression in 3T3-L1 adipocytes ref [11]. Together, current evidence suggests that Ecklonia-derived sterols and phlorotannins act as multi-target metabolic modulators spanning intestinal carbohydrate handling, insulin sensitization, hepatic lipid metabolism, and adipocyte differentiation ref [16], ref [17], ref [9], ref [11].

subsections.subsection_title: Neuroinflammation, Allergy, Tissue Protection, and Other Emerging Targets
subsections.content:
Beyond metabolic and cytoprotective indications, Ecklonia species are increasingly supported in neuroinflammatory and immunological settings. In neuronal and glial models, dieckol protected SH-SY5Y dopaminergic cells from rotenone toxicity by lowering reactive oxygen species, reducing cytochrome c release, and attenuating α-synuclein aggregation, pointing to relevance for Parkinson’s disease-related oxidative proteotoxicity ref [13]. Complementing this neuron-centered view, dieckol also suppressed microglia-mediated neurotoxicity in BV-2 and co-culture systems through inhibition of ERK, Akt, and NADPH oxidase/gp91phox-associated signaling, thereby reducing inflammatory activation and secondary neuronal death ref [15]. At the organism level, crude E. cava extract additionally reduced mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity in postoperative and neuropathic pain models in rats, suggesting that neuroimmune modulation may translate into functional analgesic benefit ref [20].

Anti-allergic activity is another recurrent theme. Extracts of E. stolonifera inhibited degranulation in RBL-2H3 cells and suppressed multiple allergy-related enzymes, including COX-2, lipoxygenase, phospholipase A2, and hyaluronidase; loss of activity after phenolic depletion implicated phlorotannins as major effectors ref [7]. At the compound level, dieckol from E. cava suppressed IgE-mediated mast-cell activation, reduced β-hexosaminidase and histamine release, downregulated FcεRI expression, and diminished passive cutaneous anaphylaxis in vivo ref [17]. These findings align with earlier reports that Ecklonia phlorotannins can modulate FcεRI-dependent allergic signaling and mast-cell/basophil responses.

Other emerging targets include systemic hyperinflammation and tissue injury. A phlorotannin-rich E. cava extract improved survival in lipopolysaccharide-induced septic shock, attenuated liver and kidney injury, and lowered NO, PGE2, HMGB-1, TNF-α, and IL-6 through coordinated suppression of TAK1/NIK/IKK/IκB/NF-κB signaling and activation of Nrf2/HO-1; dieckol reproduced much of this protection in vivo ref [11]. Collectively, these studies broaden the pharmacological scope of Ecklonia from antioxidant support to modulation of neuroinflammation, allergy, pain, and acute inflammatory tissue damage, while also highlighting the need for mechanism-driven validation in clinically relevant models.

subsections.section_title: Bioactive Compounds Isolated from Ecklonia Species
subsections.subsection_title: Anti-Infective and Antiviral Compounds from Ecklonia
subsections.content:
Among anti-infective leads from Ecklonia, antiviral activity has been most clearly demonstrated for phlorotannins from E. cava. Early mechanistic work showed that purified phlorotannins from this species inhibit HIV-1 reverse transcriptase and protease in vitro, identifying viral enzymes as plausible molecular targets rather than only nonspecific polyphenolic effects [ref 1]. Subsequent studies strengthened this concept by isolating discrete active molecules, including 6,6′-bieckol and 8,4‴-dieckol, both of which suppressed HIV-1 replication-related endpoints in cell-based systems [ref 2, ref 3].

Notably, 8,4‴-dieckol displayed activity against multiple HIV-1 strains at noncytotoxic concentrations, reducing syncytium formation, cytopathic effects, and p24 antigen production while markedly inhibiting reverse transcriptase activity; importantly, activity was retained against a triple drug-resistant RT variant, suggesting a target interaction distinct from conventional non-nucleoside RT inhibitors [ref 3]. In parallel, 6,6′-bieckol was reported to exert enhanced anti-HIV-1 efficacy, further indicating that subtle differences in phlorotannin linkage patterns influence antiviral potency [ref 2]. These findings are consistent with broader surveys highlighting marine natural products, especially algal polyphenols and sulfated polysaccharides, as a productive source of anti-HIV scaffolds [ref 4, ref 5, ref 6].

Beyond antiviral effects, Ecklonia also yields antibacterial constituents. Phlorotannins from E. kurome showed direct bactericidal activity against foodborne and clinically relevant bacteria, supporting an anti-infective role for this genus more generally [ref 7]. This antimicrobial profile aligns with the recognized bioactivity spectrum of marine algal phlorotannins, which includes membrane-active and enzyme-modulating effects [ref 8]. Overall, current evidence positions Ecklonia phlorotannins—particularly enzyme-targeting anti-HIV compounds such as 8,4‴-dieckol—as promising templates for anti-infective development, although in vivo validation, resistance profiling, and pharmacokinetic optimization remain limited [ref 1, ref 3, ref 5].

subsections.section_title: Bioactive Compounds Isolated from Ecklonia Species
subsections.subsection_title: Sulfated Polysaccharides and Other Bioactive Constituents
subsections.content:
Beyond phlorotannins, Ecklonia species contain structurally diverse sulfated polysaccharides—typically fucoidan-like, fucose-rich polymers—that represent an important parallel source of pharmacological activity. Brown-algal sulfated polysaccharides are generally characterized by variable backbones, branching patterns, sulfate substitution, and molecular weights, all of which strongly influence bioactivity ref [4]. In Ecklonia, earlier structural work on E. kurome established that fucose-containing sulfated polysaccharides exhibit pronounced anticoagulant and antithrombin activities, with activity depending on sulfate content and polymer size rather than monosaccharide composition alone ref [4].

Work on E. cava further shows that extraction strategy substantially affects the yield and composition of these polysaccharides. Enzyme-assisted extraction enriched fucose- and sulfate-containing fractions, and the Protamex-derived crude polysaccharide displayed the strongest antiproliferative effect against CT-26 colon carcinoma cells ref [24]. Mechanistically, this E. cava sulfated polysaccharide induced apoptotic body formation, increased the sub-G1 population, activated caspase-9 and PARP cleavage, and shifted the Bax/Bcl-2 balance toward apoptosis ref [24]. Purification of the active fraction further increased fucose and sulfate content and enhanced growth inhibition, supporting a composition-activity relationship ref [24].

These findings align with broader marine-algal literature indicating that sulfated polysaccharides can exert anticoagulant, antiviral, immunomodulatory, antioxidant, and antilipidemic effects, with sulfate density, sulfation position, branching, and molecular weight serving as key determinants of function ref [4]. Accordingly, Ecklonia sulfated polysaccharides should be regarded not merely as accessory matrix carbohydrates but as major non-phenolic bioactive constituents that complement the better-studied phlorotannin fraction and expand the therapeutic scope of the genus ref [4], ref [24].

subsections.section_title: Bioactive Compounds Isolated from Ecklonia Species
subsections.subsection_title: Applied Functional Effects of Ecklonia Bioactives
subsections.content:
Beyond infection- and metabolism-oriented pharmacology, Ecklonia bioactives have also been explored for applied functional outcomes relevant to quality of life and cosmeceutical development. A notable clinical example is a prospective randomized placebo-controlled trial in which a formulation containing Ecklonia bicyclis, Tribulus terrestris, and glucosamine oligosaccharide significantly improved total IIEF-15 scores, intercourse satisfaction, orgasmic function, sexual desire, overall satisfaction, ejaculation-related outcomes, and sexual quality-of-life indices in men with mild-to-moderate erectile dysfunction; benefits were particularly evident in patients with moderate arterial dysfunction, suggesting a functional vascular component to the response ref [25].

Dermatologic application has likewise emerged as a practical extension of Ecklonia research. In cultured human hair follicles and in C57BL/6 mice, an ethyl acetate fraction of Ecklonia cava promoted dermal papilla cell and outer root sheath cell proliferation, enhanced hair-shaft elongation, and accelerated telogen-to-anagen transition; mechanistically, these effects were associated with increased IGF-1 expression ref [26]. The isolated phlorotannin dioxinodehydroeckol reproduced key aspects of this activity, supporting the view that defined Ecklonia constituents can underlie measurable hair-growth-promoting effects ref [26].

Taken together, these studies illustrate how the broad antioxidant, endothelial-supporting, and growth-factor-modulating properties of Ecklonia extracts can be translated into application-oriented outcomes, spanning men’s sexual health and hair-growth promotion ref [25], ref [26]. Although the currently available evidence remains limited and, in the erectile dysfunction study, derives from a multi-ingredient formulation rather than Ecklonia alone, these reports highlight the translational potential of Ecklonia-derived preparations in functional foods, nutraceuticals, and cosmeceutical products ref [25], ref [26].

subsections.section_title: Bioactive Compounds Isolated from Ecklonia Species
subsections.content:
Phlorotannins are the signature polyphenols of Ecklonia species and are biosynthetically derived from phloroglucinol units linked through aryl–aryl and aryl–ether bonds. Early phytochemical work on Ecklonia kurome established eckol as a foundational scaffold, notable for its dibenzo-1,4-dioxin framework and for helping define the structural diversity of marine phlorotannins in this genus ref [28]. Subsequent studies further expanded this chemotype by identifying more complex oligomers, including phlorofucofuroeckol A, which uniquely incorporates both dibenzo-1,4-dioxin and dibenzofuran elements, thereby illustrating the high degree of oxidative coupling and cyclization achievable in Ecklonia metabolites ref [29].

Ecklonia stolonifera has likewise proven to be a rich source of structurally varied phlorotannins. In addition to the known compounds eckol, phlorofucofuroeckol A, and dieckol, a new pentacyclic phlorotannin, eckstolonol, was isolated from the EtOAc-soluble fraction of the methanolic extract and structurally assigned as 5,8,13,14-tetraoxa-pentaphene-1,3,6,9,11-pentaol based on HR-FAB-MS and multidimensional NMR analyses ref [27]. This study is important not only because it added a new member to the Ecklonia phlorotannin repertoire, but also because it highlighted recurring core motifs across species, suggesting a conserved biosynthetic logic within the genus ref [27], ref [28], ref [29].

Taken together, these isolation studies show that Ecklonia phlorotannins range from relatively compact trimers such as eckol to more highly fused and extended oligomers such as phlorofucofuroeckol A and dieckol ref [27], ref [28], ref [29]. Their structural complexity underpins the broad pharmacological literature discussed in later sections, while the classical chemical work on E. kurome and E. stolonifera remains the essential basis for compound identification, chemotaxonomic comparison, and structure–activity interpretation across Ecklonia species ref [27], ref [28], ref [29].

subsections.section_title: Bioactive Compounds Isolated from Ecklonia Species
subsections.subsection_title: Antioxidant, Metabolic, and Enzyme-Modulating Activities of Ecklonia Phlorotannins
subsections.content:
Ecklonia phlorotannins display a coherent spectrum of antioxidant and metabolic activities that extends beyond direct radical scavenging to transcriptional and enzymatic regulation. In particular, eckol from E. stolonifera suppresses intracellular ROS, elevates glutathione, and induces heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) expression through Nrf2 activation with upstream involvement of JNK and PI3K/Akt signaling in HepG2 cells, supporting a cytoprotective antioxidant mechanism ref [30]. Earlier work on Ecklonia extracts and related phlorotannins likewise linked these compounds to ROS reduction and hepatoprotection, indicating that redox regulation is a recurrent pharmacological theme among Ecklonia polyphenols ref [5], ref [6].

Metabolic regulation is another major axis of activity. Dieckol, one of the dominant phlorotannins of E. cava, lowers blood glucose in alloxan-induced hyperglycemic zebrafish, reduces hepatic glucose-6-phosphate and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase, and enhances Akt phosphorylation in muscle, implicating improved glucose uptake and insulin-sensitive signaling ref [31]. Complementary studies have shown that dieckol inhibits α-glucosidase and α-amylase and alleviates postprandial hyperglycemia in streptozotocin-induced diabetic mice, while other Ecklonia phlorotannins inhibit protein tyrosine phosphatase 1B, further supporting antidiabetic potential through both digestive-enzyme and intracellular signaling mechanisms ref [32], ref [7].

Phlorotannins from Ecklonia also modulate enzymes relevant to cardiometabolic homeostasis. From E. stolonifera, eckol, dieckol, and especially phlorofucofuroeckol A inhibit angiotensin-converting enzyme I, while the same study also documented strong peroxynitrite-scavenging activity, suggesting convergence of antihypertensive and antioxidant actions ref [4]. Together, these findings indicate that Ecklonia phlorotannins act as multitarget small molecules capable of coupling redox control with glucose metabolism and enzyme inhibition, thereby providing a mechanistic basis for their broader pharmacological value in oxidative stress-linked metabolic disorders.

In summary, recent pharmacological studies establish Ecklonia species as a rich source of multifunctional marine bioactives, particularly phlorotannins, sterols, and sulfated polysaccharides, with activities spanning metabolic regulation, neuroprotection, anti-inflammation, hepatoprotection, radioprotection, and vascular modulation [1–6]. Across Ecklonia cava, E. stolonifera, E. bicyclis, and E. kurome, compounds such as dieckol, eckol, fucosterol, and related phlorotannins repeatedly converge on antioxidant, anti-apoptotic, and enzyme-inhibitory mechanisms, supporting the broad therapeutic promise of this genus [2,4,7–10]. Early translational signals, including improvement of erectile function and other physiological endpoints in humans, further suggest that Ecklonia-derived preparations may have practical clinical value beyond preclinical proof-of-concept [11].

However, the field remains constrained by several recurring limitations. Many reports rely on crude extracts or enzyme-treated fractions with incomplete chemical standardization, making cross-study comparison difficult and obscuring structure–activity relationships [5,9,12]. Bioavailability, pharmacokinetics, intestinal metabolism, and tissue distribution of high-molecular-weight phlorotannins are still insufficiently defined, despite their central importance for efficacy translation [1,3,13]. In addition, most evidence derives from cell or small-animal models of obesity, diabetes, allergy, neurotoxicity, liver injury, or radiation damage, whereas robust dose-ranging, chronic toxicity, and mechanism-validated in vivo studies remain relatively limited [6,8,10,12,14].

Future work should prioritize chemotype-resolved profiling across species and harvest conditions, standardized extract manufacturing, and rigorous linkage of individual constituents to molecular targets. Integrating omics, gut microbiome analysis, and advanced formulation strategies may clarify whether native phlorotannins or their metabolites drive systemic effects [1,3,13,15]. Equally important are well-designed randomized clinical trials for indications with the strongest preclinical rationale, alongside safety assessment, drug–nutrient interaction studies, and regulatory quality benchmarks [11,16]. Such efforts will be essential to move Ecklonia research from promising marine pharmacology toward reproducible nutraceutical and therapeutic development.
